extracted.intended_audience: media critics, journalists, and engaged news consumers (readers of media watchdog commentary)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing standards for truthful reporting and ethical conduct in journalism, especially regarding claims about having reported from war zones and use of anecdotes to justify state power. Includes expectations for employers, factchecking, and contextual reporting on atrocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical journalists should not claim false combat reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: "it's not something an ethical journalist would do." (in reference to boasting of being in an 'active war zone' when one was not)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of having 'survived a combat situation' or having reported from an 'active war zone' must be factually accurate and supported by contemporaneous reporting/evidence; boasting about such experiences when inaccurate is unethical. Examples: Brian Williams' helicopter claim and Bill O'Reilly's Falklands/Argentina assertions are discussed as breaches of this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate personal-aggrandizement lies from lies that serve power
rubrics_metrics.description: "It does matter when journalists have a propensity to make things up, even for personal aggrandizement. But there's a more important level of lying when it's done in the service of power, particularly to justify state violence..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate falsehoods by their consequences: personal embellishments are problematic, but fabrications used to legitimize state violence or policy carry much greater ethical and public-interest weight and should be treated accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employers must respond to reporters' fabrications
rubrics_metrics.description: If a journalist lied about being under fire, that reflects on him—and his employers, if they decline to do anything about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations have a responsibility to investigate, correct, and take appropriate personnel action when reporters fabricate or seriously misrepresent events; failure to do so damages institutional credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fabricate or embellish anecdotal reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not make things up for personal aggrandizement (e.g., inventing rescue stories, exaggerated descriptions of 'leveled' villages or 'carnage').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes used to enhance a reporter's stature must be verifiable; the article cites O'Reilly's Meanguera description versus the actual 1982 report as an anti-pattern where embellishment altered the story's meaning and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accurate contextual reporting on atrocities and state violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective reporting that downplays or reframes atrocities can amount to complicity; failing to investigate or contextualize events like El Mozote obscures responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should situate stories about conflict within broader factual context (e.g., nearby massacres, actor responsibility). The piece criticizes O'Reilly's 'feel-good' report that omitted El Mozote's massacre, producing a 'Triumph of the Will' quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent and precise about where and when coverage occurred
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrepancies about locations/timing of coverage (e.g., claiming coverage 'in the Falklands' vs being in Buenos Aires) are substantive and undermine credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists must be clear about the geography and timing of their reporting; readers and editors should verify such claims against contemporaneous records rather than accepting after-the-fact reinterpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify claims of professional honors and awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims such as 'We won Peabody Awards' must be factual—O'Reilly/Inside Edition had not won a Peabody despite his statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award claims are easily checkable and should be verified; false claims about honors are an indicator of broader credibility problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on contemporaneous evidence (video/archives) over retrospective assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Archival video and original reports should be used to test later claims (e.g., the cited video did not show soldiers shooting at protesters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When disputed assertions arise, evaluate them against original footage, packages, and documents rather than accepting memory-based or retrospective explanations; the piece uses Mother Jones and archived CBS reports to test O'Reilly's accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish false memory from deliberate fabrication in assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial attempts to explain journalist misstatements as 'mistaken memory' should be scrutinized; more than a simple denial is often required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether errors stem from faulty memory or intentional deception by considering frequency, pattern, contemporaneous records, and motive—citing the NYT's treatment of Brian Williams as an example of inadequate parsing between mistake and fabrication.
